sentences.sentence: Generic name: apixaban [ a-PIX-a-ban ] Brand names: Eliquis , Eliquis Sprinkle , Eliquis Starter Pack for Treatment of DVT and PE Dosage forms: oral powder for reconstitution (0.15 mg), oral tablet (2.5 mg; 5 mg), oral tablet, dispersible (0.5 mg) Drug class: Factor Xa inhibitors
Medically reviewed by Drugs.com on Dec 10, 2025.
Written by Cerner Multum .
Apixaban is used to lower the risk of stroke and blood clots in adults with a heart rhythm disorder called atrial fibrillation not caused by a heart valve problem.
Apixaban is also used in adults to treat blood clots in the legs (DVT) or lungs (PE) and to lower your risk of happening again after you have received treatment for blood clots.
Apixaban is also used in adults after hip or knee replacement surgery to prevent clots that can occur in the legs ( deep vein thrombosis , DVT) or in the lungs ( pulmonary embolism , PE).

Apixaban is also used in children from birth to less than 18 years of age to treat blood clots in the legs (DVT) or lungs (PE) and lower the risk of happening again after receiving treatment for at least 5 days.
Apixaban is not approved for use in children who weigh less than 5.7 pounds (2.6 kg).
Apixaban may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction : hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Also seek emergency medical attention if you have symptoms of a spinal blood clot : back pain , numbness, tingling, muscle weakness in your lower body, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Apixaban can cause you to bleed more easily.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of bleeding such as:
bruising or bleeding that will not stop, unusual bleeding (nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vaginal bleeding);

Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Do not stop taking apixaban unless your doctor tells you to.
Stopping suddenly can increase your risk of blood clot or stroke.
Some drugs can increase your risk of bleeding when used with apixaban.
Tell your doctor about all other medicines you use.

Call your doctor at once if you have signs of bleeding such as: easy bruising, unusual bleeding, unexpected pain or swelling, feeling very weak or dizzy, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, heavy menstrual bleeding, blood in your urine or stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or any bleeding that will not stop.
Apixaban can cause a very serious blood clot around your spinal cord if you undergo a spinal tap or receive spinal anesthesia (epidural).
Tell any doctor who treats you that you are taking apixaban.
You should not take apixaban if you are allergic to it or if you have active bleeding from any cause.
Apixaban can cause a serious blood clot if you undergo a procedure such as a spinal tap or receive spinal anesthesia (epidural).
This type of blood clot could cause permanent or long-term paralysis.
Apixaban can make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury.
Call your doctor if you have any bleeding that will not stop.

It is not known if apixaban will harm an unborn baby.
Taking apixaban during pregnancy may cause bleeding in the mother or the unborn baby.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Do not breastfeed while taking apixaban.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Apixaban is usually taken twice per day.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine.
If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, you may crush it and mix the medicine with a small amount of applesauce, apple juice, or water.
If your child is prescribed the tablets for oral suspension , it should be mixed with water, infant formula, apple juice, or apple sauce.
Do not swallow the tablet.
If your child is taking capsules for oral suspension , the capsule should be opened and mixed with water or infant formula only.
Do not swallow the capsule.
Mixed medicine should be used right away .
Apixaban may also be given through a feeding tube.
apixaban can also make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury such as a fall or a bump on the head.
Tell your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you fall or hit your head, or have any bleeding that will not stop.
If you have a planned surgery or dental procedure, your doctor may tell you to stop taking apixaban for a short time.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
If your child vomits within 30 minutes after taking apixaban, take another dose.
If the child vomits after more than 30 minutes of taking apixaban, do not take another dose and give the next dose as scheduled.
Do not change your dose or stop taking apixaban unless your doctor tells you to.
If you stop taking apixaban for any reason, your doctor may prescribe another medicine to prevent blood clots.
Keep all follow-up visits with your healthcare provider.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

Xarelto (rivaroxaban) and Eliquis (apixaban) are novel anticoagulants that make blood less likely to clot (also called thinning the blood).
Both belong to the class of medicines known as factor Xa (FXa) inhibitors and they are two of the most popular blood thinners on the market.
Either one may be used to reduce the risk of stroke or treat and prevent blood clots in conditions such as DVT.

Medication-induced hair loss represents a significant concern for patients across multiple therapeutic categories.

While chemotherapy drugs are most commonly associated with severe hair loss, many commonly prescribed medications-including antibiotics, psychiatric drugs, cardiovascular agents, and hormonal therapies-can also cause this distressing side effect.
There is no longer an FDA-approved antidote for Xarelto (rivaroxaban) in the United States.
Andexxa, the only approved reversal drug, was pulled from the U.S. market on December 22, 2025, after the FDA decided its risks outweighed its benefits.
